title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

problem.description:
You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0.

Example 1:

Input: prices = [7,1,5,3,6,4]
Output: 5
Explanation: Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 6), profit = 6-1 = 5.
Note that buying on day 2 and selling on day 1 is not allowed because you must buy before you sell.

Example 2:

Input: prices = [7,6,4,3,1]
Output: 0
Explanation: In this case, no transactions are done and the max profit = 0.

Constraints:

- 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5

- 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4

hints: You pick one day to buy and a strictly later day to sell, and want the largest `sell price - buy price`. If no later price is ever higher than an earlier one, you simply do not trade and the answer is 0.

In Example 1 the best sale (price 6 at index 4) is paired with the cheapest price that came before it (1 at index 1). For any sell day, the best buy day is the cheapest earlier day; the global minimum is useless if it comes after the sale, as in `[2,4,1]` where the answer is 2, not 3.
With `prices.length` up to `10^5`, checking every buy/sell pair is about `5·10^9` operations, far too slow. You need a single linear pass, `O(n)`.
This is a prefix-minimum (one-state DP) pattern: as you sweep left to right, the best buy for today depends only on a summary of the days before it, which can be updated in constant time per day.

Fix the sell day `i`: the best profit from selling then is `prices[i] - min(prices[0..i-1])`. The answer is the largest of these values (or 0), and the prefix minimum can be maintained incrementally instead of recomputed.
Track two numbers: `minPrice`, the cheapest price on the days before the current one (starts as `prices[0]`), and `best`, the largest profit found so far (starts at 0).

Set `minPrice` to `prices[0]` and `best` to 0.
For each day `i` from 1 to `n - 1`:
Compute `profit = prices[i] - minPrice`.
If `profit` is larger than `best`, store it in `best`.
If `prices[i]` is lower than `minPrice`, store it in `minPrice`.
Return `best`.

Never reset `best` when a new minimum appears (in `[3,8,1,2]` the answer stays 5), and start `best` at 0 so falling prices like Example 2 return 0. A single day `[5]` skips the loop and returns 0, and equal prices give 0 because the profit is never greater than 0. Time is `O(n)` and extra space is `O(1)`.

normal.note: The global minimum 1 comes late; the best pair is 2 then 9.
The minimum is on the last day, so max(prices) - min(prices) = 3 would be wrong.
A new minimum 3 appears after an early small gain and leads to the best sale at 90.
Prices fall first, then rise: buy at the bottom 5 and sell at the peak 11.
Several dips and peaks; buy at 2 and sell at 8 beats every adjacent swing.

edge.note: Single day: there is no later day to sell, so the answer is 0.
Strictly decreasing: every trade loses money, so not trading gives 0.
All equal: every profit is 0, so the answer is 0.
Two days, increasing: the only possible trade earns 1.
Value bounds: buy at the minimum price 0 and sell at the maximum 10^4.
Strictly increasing: buy on the first day and sell on the last; at n = 10^5 this still needs an O(n) pass.

approach.oneLiner: Choose a buy day `i` and a later sell day `j` to maximise `prices[j] - prices[i]`, returning 0 if no such pair makes money.
signals: "choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock" → only earlier days can be the buy day for a given sell day, so each day needs a summary of the prefix before it.
"a single day to buy ... a different day ... to sell" → exactly one pair, so the answer is the best over sell days of the price minus the cheapest earlier price.
"1 <= prices.length <= 10^5" → checking all `n(n - 1)/2` pairs is about `5·10^9`, so one linear pass is needed.
"If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0" → start the answer at 0; falling prices like Example 2 must return 0, not a negative number.
approach.constraints: With `n = 10^5`, all pairs is `n(n - 1)/2 ≈ 5·10^9` checks, far too slow; sorting would destroy the day order anyway. One pass is `10^5` constant-time steps, so the target is `O(n)` time and ideally `O(1)` extra space.

thinking.q: What is the simplest correct method?
thinking.a: Try every buy day `i` and every later sell day `j`, keeping the largest `prices[j] - prices[i]`. Example 1 has 15 pairs, and the best is `6 - 1 = 5`.

thinking.q: If I fix the sell day `j`, which buy day should I pair it with?
thinking.a: The cheapest day before `j`, because a lower buy price always means more profit for the same sell price. For selling at 6 (index 4) in Example 1, the cheapest earlier price is 1 (index 1), which is the statement's "buy on day 2, sell on day 5" in 1-based days.

thinking.q: Why not just buy at the global minimum and sell at the global maximum?
thinking.a: The minimum may come after the maximum. In `[2,4,1]` the global minimum 1 is the last day, so the real answer is `4 - 2 = 2`, not `4 - 1 = 3`.

thinking.q: How do I get the cheapest earlier price for every day without rescanning?
thinking.a: The cheapest price on days `0..i` is `min(cheapest on days 0..i-1, prices[i])`, so a prefix-minimum array `minLeft` can be filled in one left-to-right pass.

thinking.q: Do I need to keep the whole `minLeft` array?
thinking.a: No. Day `i` only reads `minLeft[i - 1]`, once. So a single variable `minPrice` works: compute today's profit against it, then lower it if today is cheaper. That gives `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space.

approaches.name: Check every buy/sell pair
approaches.aha: The answer is the largest `prices[j] - prices[i]` over pairs with `i < j`, so the obvious first move is to try every pair of days.
approaches.idea: An outer loop picks the buy day `i` and an inner loop tries every later sell day `j`, computing `prices[j] - prices[i]` and keeping the largest value in `best`. Starting `best` at 0 covers the case where every pair loses money, as in Example 2. It is correct because it examines every legal transaction, so the maximum cannot be missed.
steps: For each buy day `i` from 0 to `n - 2`, read `buy = prices[i]`.
For each sell day `j` from `i + 1` to `n - 1`, compute `profit = prices[j] - buy`.
If `profit` is larger than `best`, store it in `best`.
approaches.complexity: The nested loops examine `n(n - 1)/2` pairs with `O(1)` work each, which dominates everything else. Only a few scalars are stored, so extra space is `O(1)`.
approaches.tradeoff: For `n = 10^5` that is about `5·10^9` pairs, far beyond the time limit. For every sell day it effectively rescans all earlier days to find the cheapest one, repeating the same minimum search again and again.

pseudocode: best ← 0  // not trading is allowed, so the answer is never below 0
for i ← 0 to n - 2  // buy on day i
for j ← i + 1 to n - 1  // sell on a strictly later day j
best ← profit  // new best pair (i, j)

parts.why: Every day except the last is tried as the buy day.

parts.cost: n − 1 − i iterations × O(1) for buy day i
parts.why: Every later day is tried as the sell day, with a subtraction and a comparison each.

time.sum: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 = O(n^2); the inner loop dominates the O(n) outer loop.
time.feel: n = 10^5 → about 5·10^9 pair checks, several seconds even in C++, so it gets Time Limit Exceeded.

parts.part: Scalars n, best, i, buy, j, sell, profit (lines 2-8)
parts.why: A fixed number of variables regardless of n.

space.note: The input prices is only read and the output is a single integer.

steps.explain: There are n = 6 days and no trade has been made, so best = 0.
Buy day i = 0 (price 7), sell day j = 1 (price 1): profit = 1 - 7 = -6, which is not > 0, so best stays 0.
Skipping j = 2..4 for i = 0: profits 5-7, 3-7 and 6-7 are all negative. At j = 5 profit = 4 - 7 = -3; buying at 7 never pays, best stays 0.
4 > 0, so best = 4: buying at 1 (index 1) and selling at 5 (index 2) is the best pair so far.
i = 1, j = 3: profit = 3 - 1 = 2, not > 4; best stays 4.
5 > 4, so best = 5: buy at 1 (index 1), sell at 6 (index 4).
i = 1, j = 5: profit = 4 - 1 = 3, not > 5. All sell days for buy index 1 are done.
Buy day i = 2 (price 5): j = 3 gives -2, j = 4 gives 1, and j = 5 gives profit = 4 - 5 = -1; none beats 5.
Buy day i = 3 (price 3): j = 4 gives 3 and j = 5 gives profit = 4 - 3 = 1; none beats 5.
Last pair: buy at 6 (index 4), sell at 4 (index 5), profit = -2; best stays 5.
All 15 pairs have been checked; return best = 5.

dryRun.result: 5 — the pair buy at 1 (index 1), sell at 6 (index 4) has the largest difference among all 15 pairs with buy before sell.

approaches.name: Prefix minimum array
approaches.aha: For a fixed sell day `j`, the brute force scans every earlier day, yet the only one that matters is the cheapest, `min(prices[0..j-1])`, and those prefix minimums can be computed for all days in one pass.
approaches.idea: Precompute `minLeft[i]`, the cheapest price on days `0..i`, with `minLeft[i] = min(minLeft[i - 1], prices[i])`. Selling on day `i` then earns at most `prices[i] - minLeft[i - 1]`, and the answer is the largest of these values, or 0. This is correct because for a fixed sell price a lower buy price always gives a higher profit, so the cheapest earlier day is the best partner for every sell day.
steps: Create `minLeft` of length `n` and set `minLeft[0] = prices[0]`.
For `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, set `minLeft[i]` to the smaller of `minLeft[i - 1]` and `prices[i]`.
For each sell day `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, compute `profit = prices[i] - minLeft[i - 1]`.
Keep the largest `profit` in `best`, then return `best`.
approaches.complexity: Two separate linear passes, one to build `minLeft` and one to evaluate each sell day, give `O(n)` time. The `minLeft` array of length `n` is the extra memory.
approaches.tradeoff: It meets the time limit, but it stores `n` prefix minimums even though each `minLeft[i - 1]` is read exactly once, right when day `i` is processed.

pseudocode: minLeft ← array of n values  // minLeft[i] = cheapest price on days 0..i
minLeft[i] ← min(minLeft[i - 1], prices[i])  // extend the prefix by one day
profit ← prices[i] - minLeft[i - 1]  // sell on day i, buy at the cheapest earlier day

parts.why: Each minLeft[i] is one min of two numbers.
Each sell day does one subtraction and one comparison.

time.sum: (n − 1) + (n − 1) = 2n − 2 = O(n); two linear passes stay linear.
time.feel: n = 10^5 → about 2·10^5 simple steps, well under a millisecond.

parts.why: One prefix minimum is stored per day.

space.sum: n + O(1) = O(n); the minLeft array dominates.
space.note: The input prices is not counted.

steps.explain: Allocate minLeft (unfilled cells shown as -) and set minLeft[0] = prices[0] = 7: at index 0 the only price seen is 7.
i = 1: minLeft[1] = min(minLeft[0] 7, prices[1] 1) = 1; index 1 is the new cheapest day.
i = 2: minLeft[2] = min(1, 5) = 1; 5 is not cheaper, so the minimum stays 1.
i = 3..5 (skipped to the last one): prices 3, 6 and 4 are all above 1, so minLeft[3], minLeft[4] and minLeft[5] all stay 1. minLeft = [7, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1].
minLeft is complete. Start best at 0, the profit of not trading.
i = 1: profit = prices[1] - minLeft[0] = 1 - 7 = -6; selling at index 1 loses money, best stays 0.
i = 2: profit = prices[2] - minLeft[1] = 5 - 1 = 4 > previous best, so best = 4.
i = 3: profit = prices[3] - minLeft[2] = 3 - 1 = 2, not > 4; best stays 4.
i = 4: profit = prices[4] - minLeft[3] = 6 - 1 = 5 > previous best, so best = 5.
i = 5: profit = prices[5] - minLeft[4] = 4 - 1 = 3, not > 5; best stays 5.
Every sell day was paired with its cheapest earlier day; return best = 5.

dryRun.result: 5 — minLeft = [7,1,1,1,1,1], and the best sell day is index 4: prices[4] - minLeft[3] = 6 - 1 = 5.

approaches.name: One pass with a running minimum
approaches.aha: Since `minLeft[i - 1]` is only needed at day `i`, we can keep just the latest prefix minimum in one variable `minPrice` and fold both passes into one.
approaches.idea: Scan the days left to right, holding `minPrice` (the cheapest price on the days before `i`) and `best` (the best profit so far). On day `i`, first try selling: `profit = prices[i] - minPrice`, and raise `best` if it is larger. Then let day `i` become a buy candidate by lowering `minPrice` if `prices[i]` is cheaper. The invariant is that when day `i` is examined, `minPrice = min(prices[0..i-1])`, so every sell day is paired with its best buy day, exactly as in the prefix-array version.
steps: For each day `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, compute `profit = prices[i] - minPrice`.
If `profit` is larger than `best`, store it in `best`.
If `prices[i]` is smaller than `minPrice`, store it in `minPrice`.
approaches.complexity: One loop over `n - 1` days with constant work per day gives `O(n)` time. Only `minPrice`, `best` and `profit` are stored, so extra space is `O(1)`.
approaches.tradeoff: Every price must be read at least once, since any unread day could be a new minimum or a better sale, so `O(n)` time is optimal, and `O(1)` space cannot be improved.

pseudocode: minPrice ← prices[0]  // cheapest buy price seen so far
best ← 0  // not trading is allowed, so the answer is never negative
profit ← prices[i] - minPrice  // best profit if we sell on day i
minPrice ← prices[i]  // later sell days can buy at this cheaper price

parts.why: Each day does one subtraction and at most two comparisons and two assignments.

time.feel: n = 10^5 → 10^5 iterations, well under a millisecond.

parts.part: Scalars n, minPrice, best, i, profit (lines 2-6)
parts.why: No array is built; the prefix minimum lives in one variable.

space.note: The input prices is only read and the output is a single integer.

steps.explain: Day 0 is the only day seen, so minPrice = prices[0] = 7 and best = 0.
i = 1: profit = prices[1] - minPrice = 1 - 7 = -6; selling at index 1 would lose money, so best stays 0.
prices[1] = 1 is below the old minPrice 7, so minPrice = 1: every later day can now buy at 1.
i = 2: profit = prices[2] - minPrice = 5 - 1 = 4, which is greater than best = 0.
So best = 4: selling at 5 (index 2) after buying at 1 is the best trade so far; 5 is not a new minimum, so minPrice will stay 1.
i = 3: profit = 3 - 1 = 2, not > 4. Price 3 is not below minPrice 1, so nothing else changes.
i = 4: profit = prices[4] - minPrice = 6 - 1 = 5, which is greater than best = 4.
So best = 5: selling at 6 (index 4) after buying at 1 is the best trade so far; 6 is not a new minimum, so minPrice will stay 1.
i = 5: profit = 4 - 1 = 3, not > 5, and 4 is not a new minimum. The loop ends.
Return best = 5.

dryRun.result: 5 — minPrice became 1 at index 1, and selling at 6 at index 4 gave the largest profit 6 - 1 = 5; no later day did better.

mistakes: Returning `max(prices) - min(prices)` while ignoring the order of days: `[2,4,1]` gives 3, but the minimum comes after the maximum, so the real answer is 2.
Starting `best` at `INT_MIN` or at `prices[1] - prices[0]`: for falling prices such as Example 2 this returns a negative number instead of 0.
Resetting `best` when a new minimum price appears: in `[3,8,1,2]` the profit 5 from buying at 3 must survive even after `minPrice` drops to 1.
Summing every positive day-to-day rise, which solves the unlimited-transactions version: `[1,2,3,1,5]` would give 6, but with one transaction the answer is 4.
edgeCases: `prices = [5]`: the loop never runs, so the answer is 0; reading `prices[0]` is safe because `prices.length >= 1`.
Strictly decreasing prices like `[9,7,4,1]`: every profit is negative, so `best` must stay at its starting value 0.
All equal prices like `[3,3,3,3]`: every profit is exactly 0, and since `0 > 0` is false, `best` stays 0.
A new minimum after the best pair, like `[3,8,1,2]`: `minPrice` drops to 1 but the answer is still 5, which catches solutions that reset `best`.

related.title: Maximum Subarray
related.why: Kadane's algorithm keeps a running best in one pass; this problem is the maximum subarray sum of the day-to-day price differences.

related.title: Maximum Difference Between Increasing Elements
related.why: Almost the same task, `max nums[j] - nums[i]` with `i < j` and `nums[i] < nums[j]`, solved with the same running minimum.

takeaways: For "best pair with `i < j`" problems, fix the right end `j` and ask what the best left partner is; that turns an `O(n^2)` pair search into a prefix query.
A prefix array that is only read at the current index can be collapsed into one running variable, cutting space from `O(n)` to `O(1)`.
Initialise the answer to the value of "doing nothing" (here 0) when the problem allows not acting.
Order of updates inside a one-pass loop matters: use the state of the earlier days before letting the current day update it.
